section.title: Community Laws
section.sectionRationale: This chapter fences the worshipping community and the camp with holiness: who may join the assembly, purity in the camp where the LORD walks, protection for a runaway slave, a ban on cultic prostitution, honest lending among brothers, and the seriousness of a vow, showing that covenant holiness touches worship, camp life, economics, and everyday speech alike.
section.thesis: Because the LORD Himself walks among His people, this chapter protects the purity of Israel's worshipping assembly and camp, extends unusual mercy to a runaway slave and the poor brother needing an interest-free loan, and insists that a vow, once spoken to the LORD, must be kept.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: who may and may not enter the assembly of the LORD; the purity of the camp, since the LORD walks there; protection for a slave who has taken refuge; the ban on shrine prostitution and its wages; the ban on charging a brother interest; the requirement to keep a vow once made; and the right to eat, but not harvest, from a neighbor's field.

verses.text: No man with crushed or severed genitals may enter the assembly of the LORD.
No one of illegitimate birth may enter the assembly of the LORD, nor may any of his descendants, even to the tenth generation.
No Ammonite or Moabite or any of their descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD, even to the tenth generation.
For they did not meet you with food and water on your way out of Egypt, and they hired Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you.
Yet the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam, and the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loves you.
You are not to seek peace or prosperity from them as long as you live.
Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother. Do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land.
The third generation of children born to them may enter the assembly of the LORD.
When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every wicked thing.
If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, he must leave the camp and stay outside.
When evening approaches, he must wash with water, and when the sun sets he may return to the camp.
You must have a place outside the camp to go and relieve yourself.
And you must have a digging tool in your equipment so that when you relieve yourself you can dig a hole and cover up your excrement.
For the LORD your God walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you. Your camp must be holy, lest He see anything unclean among you and turn away from you.

units.label: A refuge for the runaway slave

verses.text: Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you.
Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing. Do not oppress him.
No daughter or son of Israel is to be a {{qedeshah|shrine prostitute}}.
You must not bring the wages of a prostitute, whether female or male, into the house of the LORD your God to fulfill any vow, because both are detestable to the LORD your God.

units.label: No interest on a brother's loan

verses.text: Do not charge your brother {{neshekh|interest}} on money, food, or any other type of loan.
You may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother, so that the LORD your God may bless you in everything to which you put your hand in the land that you are entering to possess.

units.label: Keep your vow
units.note: optional to make, required to keep

verses.text: If you make a {{neder|vow}} to the LORD your God, do not be slow to keep it, because He will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin.
But if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin.
Be careful to follow through on what comes from your lips, because you have freely vowed to the LORD your God with your own mouth.
When you enter your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes, but you must not put any in your basket.
When you enter your neighbor's grainfield, you may pluck the heads of grain with your hand, but you must not put a sickle to your neighbor's grain.

qedeshah.gloss: Shrine prostitute, literally built on the Hebrew word for 'holy' or 'set apart.' Canaanite fertility religion twisted the language of holiness into cultic sex; Israel's own worship was to have absolutely nothing to do with it.

neshekh.gloss: Interest, literally a 'bite,' from a root meaning to bite. Charging interest to a needy brother was forbidden, since the loan was meant as an act of covenant kindness, not a source of profit.

neder.gloss: Vow, a freely made promise to the LORD. Making a vow was entirely optional, but once spoken it had to be kept fully and without delay.

basic.context: This chapter sets boundaries for who may join Israel's worshipping assembly, requires the war camp to be kept ritually clean because the LORD Himself walks there, protects a runaway slave from being returned to bondage, forbids the cultic prostitution common in Canaanite religion, bans charging interest to a needy brother, and insists that a vow, once made, must be kept exactly.
basic.hermeneutics: These specific exclusions, purity rules, and economic laws describe Israel's particular old covenant community. Some, like the assembly exclusions, are later reversed in principle by the gospel's welcome of the nations and the eunuch (Isaiah 56:3-5; Acts 8:26-39), while the underlying concerns, protecting worship's integrity, honest speech, and generosity to the poor, remain.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel's own worship must never adopt the qedeshah, shrine prostitute, of Canaanite religion, a term ironically built on the word for 'holy.' Loans to a needy brother must carry no neshekh, interest, literally a 'bite.' And a neder, vow, once spoken to the LORD, must be kept fully.
basic.typology: The runaway slave who finds refuge and must not be returned to his master pictures the gospel's welcome of every fugitive from sin who flees to God for shelter, rather than being sent back into bondage.
basic.christ: Isaiah 56:3-5 promises that the very eunuch excluded from the assembly in this chapter will one day be given 'a name better than sons and daughters' in God's house, a promise fulfilled when Philip baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8:26-39, the gospel deliberately reversing this chapter's exclusion in Christ.
basic.god: God cares that His worshipping community remains pure and honest, yet He is also the God who, in time, welcomes the outsider, the eunuch, the foreigner, the very categories fenced out here, showing His ultimate purpose was always to widen the gate through the gospel.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 56:3-5 promises inclusion for the eunuch, reversing this chapter's exclusion. Acts 8:26-39 shows Philip baptizing the Ethiopian eunuch, fulfilling that promise. Ruth, a Moabite, becomes an ancestress of David and Christ despite this chapter's exclusion of Moabites. Galatians 3:28 says in Christ there is neither slave nor free.
basic.oneStory: The old covenant fenced the assembly and the camp with real boundaries, yet even within the Old Testament, God's grace to Ruth the Moabite hints at where the story is heading: the gospel's welcome of every nation, the eunuch, and the outsider into the one people of God in Christ.

context.literary:
This chapter organizes itself around two related questions, who or what may come near, and what is owed once someone has. The first two units, who may enter the assembly (verses 1-8) and what keeps the camp pure (verses 9-14), both concern approach to the LORD's own presence, while the remaining five units, the runaway slave, shrine prostitution, interest, vows, and eating from a neighbor's field, concern what a people who live near that presence owe to one another. Verse 14's declaration that the LORD your God walks throughout your camp sits almost exactly at the chapter's midpoint, functioning as the theological hinge that explains everything on both sides of it, purity requirements for entering His camp, and generosity and honesty appropriate to a people He personally walks among.

The opening unit is also structured by a graduated scale of exclusion that undercuts any simple reading of outsiders barred. A man with crushed or severed genitals is excluded without any stated limit; a person of illegitimate birth, and his descendants, for ten generations; Ammon and Moab, permanently, and for a stated historical reason; but Edomites and Egyptians, despite real grievance, only for three generations, with the text itself calling the Edomite your brother. The chapter relativizes its own boundaries by relationship and remembered history rather than applying one uniform rule to every outsider.

The final three units, the ban on interest, the requirement to keep a vow, and the permission to eat freely but not harvest from a neighbor's field, share a common shape, generosity is commanded, but a clear limit marks where generosity would become exploitation on one side or presumption on the other.
context.historical:
Ammon and Moab's hostility during the exodus, refusing food and water and hiring Balaam to curse Israel (verse 4, recalling Numbers 22-24), gives the chapter's harshest and longest-lasting exclusion its stated historical reason, in contrast to Edom and Egypt, whose grievances against Israel were real but are treated as nearer kin. The crushed or severed genitals of verse 1 may reflect a wider ancient Near Eastern context in which some fertility cults maintained castrated priesthoods, though the text itself gives no cultic reason, unlike its explicit reason for excluding Ammon and Moab.

The sanitation instructions of verses 12 to 13, a place outside the camp and a digging tool to cover waste, reflect ordinary practical necessity for any large group living together, yet the text gives them an explicitly theological rather than merely hygienic rationale, tied directly to the LORD's own presence walking through the camp.

The ban on charging a needy brother interest, while permitting it with a foreigner, reflects Israel's understanding of a loan to a fellow Israelite as an act of covenant solidarity with the poor rather than commercial enterprise, in a world where interest on ordinary loans was often set at rates that could quickly overwhelm a struggling household. And the command to shelter rather than return a runaway slave stands in real contrast to other ancient Near Eastern law, which typically required a fugitive's return and punished anyone caught sheltering him, making this law's protection of the powerless genuinely unusual for its time.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 56:3-8 takes up this chapter's two harshest exclusions, the eunuch and the foreigner, and promises both a welcome in God's own house, language the New Testament shows being fulfilled when Philip baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch reading that very prophecy, Acts 8:26-39. The Moabite exclusion of verse 3 receives its own quiet canonical answer even earlier, a Moabite widow named Ruth becomes King David's great-grandmother, and Matthew's genealogy carries her name straight into the ancestry of Jesus, Matthew 1:5, so that the very nation fenced out here supplies part of the Messiah's own family line.

The vow-keeping instruction of verses 21 to 23 finds an almost word for word echo in Ecclesiastes 5:4-5, better not to vow at all than to vow and fail to pay, and Jesus later presses the same concern for truthful speech even further, telling His hearers to let their yes be yes and their no be no rather than depending on oaths at all, Matthew 5:33-37, tightening rather than relaxing this chapter's demand for a word that can be trusted without reinforcement.

The picture of the LORD walking through the camp, verse 14, reaches back to Eden, where God is described walking in the garden (Genesis 3:8), and forward to the New Testament's description of the Word becoming flesh and tabernacling among His people, John 1:14, a single thread of mobile divine presence running from creation through the wilderness camp to the incarnation.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Moses wants Israel to understand that its assembly and camp belong to a God who is genuinely present among them, so both require real, practical purity, while also showing, through the graduated time limits and the named exceptions for Edom and Egypt, that these boundaries are reasoned from Israel's actual history rather than a blanket suspicion of all outsiders as such. He also intends to shape an economy and a culture of speech marked by mercy toward the powerless, sheltering a runaway slave, lending to the poor without profit, and by scrupulous honesty, refusing to let tainted wages fund worship and refusing to let a spoken vow go unpaid. Across all seven units the same conviction holds, a people who live this near to the LORD's presence cannot treat their assembly, their camp, their economy, or their own words as ordinary.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The specific exclusions from the assembly, along with the camp's sanitation rules bound to a mobile, tented, military setting, describe Israel's particular old covenant community and are not directly prescriptive for the church, which the New Testament itself explicitly and deliberately opens to the very categories excluded here, the eunuch and the foreigner chief among them. What does carry forward as an enduring concern is the ban on cultic prostitution, the refusal to profit from lending to the poor, and the requirement that a vow, once spoken, be kept exactly, since none of these rest on Israel's specific national history the way the assembly exclusions do. The instruction to eat freely but not harvest from a neighbor's field likewise carries forward as a picture of generosity bounded by honesty rather than a specific agricultural statute.

debates.question: How should Christians read the assembly exclusions of verses 1-8 in light of Isaiah 56 and Acts 8?

views.label: Old covenant boundaries later reversed in Christ
views.case: Isaiah 56:3-5 explicitly promises the eunuch a name better than sons and daughters within God's own house, and Acts 8:26-39 shows this fulfilled without hesitation, so these exclusions were bound to Israel's specific covenant community and history rather than a permanent statement about who God ultimately welcomes.

views.label: Boundaries protecting covenant identity in their own moment
views.case: In their historical setting these laws protected Israel's distinct worship against nations that had shown real hostility or embodied corrupt religion, functioning like membership boundaries protecting a young community's integrity, without settling anything final about salvation for individuals within those groups.

debates.bearing: Both views agree the boundaries belonged to that specific covenant community and moment, and that the gospel deliberately and explicitly widens the welcome to the very people once excluded, rather than quietly ignoring this chapter's own terms.

debates.question: What does the law about crushed or severed genitals in verse 1 most likely address?

views.label: A ban connected to pagan cultic castration
views.case: Some fertility religions of the wider ancient world maintained castrated priesthoods as part of their worship, and this reading places verse 1 alongside the chapter's later ban on shrine prostitution, verses 17-18, both refusing Israel's assembly to a category tied to a specific pagan religious practice rather than to physical condition as such.

views.label: A general exclusion reflecting the assembly's symbolic wholeness
views.case: The text gives no explicit cultic reason here, unlike the shrine prostitution ban a few verses later, and groups this case instead with several others, illegitimate birth, hostile nations, defined by circumstances outside a person's control, suggesting a concern for bodily wholeness in approaching the LORD similar to what disqualifies a priest with a physical defect from serving at the altar, Leviticus 21:17-20.

debates.bearing: Either way, Isaiah 56:3-5 already announces, from within the Old Testament itself, that this exclusion will not have the last word, the LORD promises the eunuch a name better than sons and daughters in His own house.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 uses a rare term, mamzer, traditionally rendered of illegitimate birth. It occurs only twice in the entire Old Testament, here and in Zechariah 9:6, where the BSB renders it a mixed race settling in Ashdod. Because the word is so rare, the safest conclusion from the text itself is only that it names some category of birth considered improper for entry into the assembly for ten generations, the same span given to Ammon and Moab in the verses that follow.

Verse 1 names two conditions with technical, almost clinical precision rather than a single general word for injury, one describing crushed genitals and the other a severed member, language that reads like a recognized medical or legal category of its own time rather than a loose figure of speech for disability in general.

Verse 14 describes the LORD walking, mithhalekh, throughout the camp, the same reflexive, ongoing form of the verb used of God walking in the garden in Genesis 3:8 and of His promise, I will walk among you, in Leviticus 26:12. The verb pictures presence in motion, not a distant deity but One who moves through the actual space His people occupy, which is exactly why the surrounding sanitation laws matter, they are practical instructions given theological weight by whose company the camp keeps.

That same verse calls the camp qadosh, holy, a word built on the same root as qedeshah, the shrine prostitute banned a few verses later. The wordplay is almost certainly intentional, Canaanite religion had already claimed the language of set apart for its cultic sex trade, and this chapter insists that true holiness belongs instead to an ordinary camp kept clean because the LORD walks through it.

Finally, neshekh, the bite of interest banned in verse 19, is regularly paired elsewhere with a second word for interest, tarbit, increase (Leviticus 25:36-37; Ezekiel 18:8, 13, 17; 22:12). Read together the two words describe usury from both sides at once, what it bites out of a poor borrower and what it adds for a lender who has no need of the extra gain, which is why the law bans it specifically toward a brother while still permitting ordinary commercial interest with a foreigner, verse 20. The vow of verse 21, neder, is simply a freely spoken promise, but the verb that follows it, shalem, to complete or repay, is the same root behind shalom, wholeness or peace, so that failing to complete a vow is pictured as leaving something owed unfinished, a debt of the mouth still outstanding before the LORD.

typology.type: The runaway slave granted refuge, Deuteronomy 23:15-16
typology.fulfillment: The law will not let Israel become an instrument returning the oppressed to their oppressor, the fugitive chooses where to live and must not be wronged. Paul tells believers they have been set free from slavery to sin and have become slaves to righteousness, Romans 6:17-18, language of a permanent change of master rather than a return to the old one. The type is limited, this law protects a runaway from one human master to relative safety among another, the gospel actually changes what a person is enslaved to, not merely where they are permitted to live.

typology.type: The eunuch excluded from the assembly, Deuteronomy 23:1
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 56:3-5 promises this very man a name better than sons and daughters within God's own house, a reversal announced centuries before it happens. Acts 8:26-39 shows Philip baptizing an Ethiopian eunuch who has just been reading Isaiah, so that both his exclusion and its reversal meet in a single scene. The type is not merely fulfilled but deliberately reversed, a category this chapter fences out becomes, in Christ, a picture of the gospel's widest welcome, given without hesitation the moment it is preached.

typology.type: The LORD walking through the camp, Deuteronomy 23:14
typology.fulfillment: God's presence here is mobile and conditional, He walks among His people but turns away from what is unclean. John says the Word became flesh and made His dwelling, literally tabernacled, among us, John 1:14, the same walking presence now permanently, personally located in Jesus. Revelation completes the picture, God Himself will be with them, with no more need for camp purity laws to keep Him from turning away, Revelation 21:3. The escalation is total, from a presence that could withdraw over uncleanness to a presence that never again departs.

typology.type: Eating freely from a neighbor's field without exploiting it, Deuteronomy 23:24-25
typology.fulfillment: The law grants a traveler real, immediate access to another's harvest while forbidding him to profit from it. Jesus' own disciples exercise exactly this right, picking heads of grain by hand as they pass through a field on the Sabbath, Matthew 12:1, and Jesus defends them by pointing past the letter of Sabbath law to what mercy requires. The correspondence is not a promise fulfilled so much as an ancient provision for generosity still operating, unquestioned, in Jesus' own day, and put to use by the very disciples who would carry His gospel to a hungry world.

study.christ:
The chapter's clearest road to Christ runs through its most severe exclusion. Verse 1 bars the eunuch from the assembly of the LORD, yet within the Old Testament's own pages Isaiah already overturns it, let not the eunuch say, I am but a dry tree, for I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters, Isaiah 56:3-5. Acts 8:26-39 shows this promise land on one particular man, an Ethiopian court official reading Isaiah on a desert road, whom Philip baptizes without hesitation. The category this law fences out becomes, in Luke's telling, one of the earliest converts recorded outside Jerusalem, and the very prophet whose scroll he was reading had already announced his welcome.

Verse 3's exclusion of Moab tells a similar story from the opposite direction. A Moabite could not enter the assembly, yet a Moabite widow named Ruth becomes David's great-grandmother, and through David, an ancestor of Jesus Himself, named outright in Matthew's genealogy, Matthew 1:5. The law's boundary and the gospel's genealogy sit inside the very same Bible, and Scripture never resolves the tension by pretending the law was mistaken, it resolves it by showing that mercy toward an individual like Ruth was always compatible with the law's larger purpose of protecting Israel's worship from real, ongoing hostility.

Christ also stands behind the chapter's picture of God's mobile presence. The LORD walks throughout your camp, verse 14, present but capable of turning away from what is unclean. John describes the Word becoming flesh and tabernacling among us, John 1:14, a presence that walks among people in an entirely new, personal way, and Revelation completes what this chapter could only picture in miniature, God Himself will be with them, permanently, with no more turning away, Revelation 21:3.

Even the runaway slave law points, faintly but really, toward the gospel's welcome of the fugitive from sin. Israel is forbidden from returning an escaped slave to bondage, Paul tells the Romans they have been freed from slavery to sin and now serve righteousness instead, Romans 6:17-18, a freedom Christ secures rather than merely permits or extends.
study.god:
This chapter presents a God who is genuinely present, not a distant lawgiver but One who walks throughout your camp, verse 14, close enough that uncleanness could cause Him to turn away. That single image holds together holiness and nearness at once, He is near enough to be affected by what is unclean, and He stays near anyway, giving detailed, unglamorous instructions, down to where to dig a latrine, so that His presence can remain among an ordinary, physical people rather than withdraw from them.

He is also, remarkably, a God whose boundaries carry their own built-in exceptions and explanations. Ammon and Moab are excluded because of specific, remembered hostility, not simply because they are foreign, while Edom and Egypt, despite real historical grievance, are to be treated with something closer to kinship, do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother, do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land, verses 7-8. God's exclusions in this chapter are reasoned from real history and real relationship, not blanket hostility toward outsiders as such.

He is a God who sides with the powerless against the powerful. The runaway slave law commands Israel to shelter, not return, a fugitive who has escaped bondage, a striking departure from the normal expectations of the ancient world, and it comes with no exception clause protecting a master's claim.

He is a God who refuses to let His own worship be paid for by exploitation or corruption. The wages of a shrine prostitute may not enter His house even to fulfill a vow, verse 18, and a poor brother's loan may not become a source of profit, verses 19-20. Even sincere religious devotion, a vow paid, a debt collected, is not permitted to launder an underlying wrong.

Finally, He is a God who takes human speech with total seriousness. A vow was never required, but once spoken it comes from your lips, verse 23, and He will hold a person to exactly what they freely said. Nothing here suggests God delights in technicalities, rather, He treats a person's own word as something too significant to be casually broken, because He Himself never breaks His.

crossReferences.note: Promises the eunuch excluded in Deuteronomy 23:1 a name better than sons and daughters within the LORD's own house, reversing this chapter's exclusion from within the Old Testament's own pages centuries before Acts.

Philip baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch who has just been reading the very prophecy that promised his welcome, showing Isaiah 56's reversal of this chapter's exclusion taking place in real, recorded apostolic history.

Names Ruth the Moabite plainly in Jesus' own genealogy, the very nation excluded from the assembly in Deuteronomy 23:3 producing, several generations later, an actual, named ancestor of the Messiah Himself.
Declares that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, the deeper theological ground for this chapter's own instinct to shelter, rather than hand back, a runaway slave to bondage and mistreatment.
God's promise, I will walk among you and be your God, uses the same Hebrew verb as Deuteronomy 23:14's description of the LORD walking through Israel's camp, tying camp purity to covenant presence.
Describes God walking in the garden in the cool of the day using the same verb form as Deuteronomy 23:14, so that Israel's camp, kept holy for His presence, deliberately echoes the garden of Eden.

Jesus' disciples pick heads of grain by hand while passing through a field on the Sabbath, exercising exactly the right this chapter grants any traveler in verses 24-25, without objection from Jesus over the act.
Gives nearly identical instruction on vows in different words, that it is better not to vow at all than to vow and fail to pay, matching Deuteronomy 23:21-23 almost point for point.

study.oneStory:
Eden was the first place where God's presence and human life shared the same space without any barrier, and Genesis pictures Him walking there in the cool of the day, Genesis 3:8, before sin sends the man and woman out and stations cherubim to guard the way back in. Deuteronomy 23 pictures a smaller, traveling version of the same arrangement, the LORD again walks among His people, this time through their camp, and again His presence requires real purity, lest He turn away, verse 14. The distance between Eden and Sinai's camp is real, but the underlying pattern, holy presence requiring a holy space, is the same pattern running through the whole story.

Within that camp, this chapter fences the worshipping assembly with real, sometimes severe boundaries, while quietly building in the very exceptions that will later widen. Edom and Egypt, despite genuine grievance, are treated as nearer than Ammon and Moab, a runaway slave finds shelter rather than being sent back, a poor brother's loan is protected from exploitation. The boundaries are never simply about keeping foreigners out, they are about protecting a still forming, still vulnerable community's worship and economy from corruption.

The rest of the Bible does not quietly drop this chapter's exclusions, it deliberately answers them. A Moabite widow becomes David's ancestor and Christ's. A prophet promises the excluded eunuch a place and a name better than sons and daughters. An apostle baptizes exactly that man on a desert road. What Deuteronomy 23 fences, Isaiah and Acts reopen, not by contradicting the Torah but by revealing where its own logic, mercy toward the vulnerable, honesty in worship, a presence that walks among ordinary people, was always heading.

The story ends where it began, with God's presence and human life sharing the same space again, this time without any conditions left to violate. Revelation pictures no more camp to purify and no more distance to bridge, the dwelling place of God is with man, He will dwell with them, Revelation 21:3, the walking presence of Eden and the camp become, at last, a permanent home.

quiz.q: Why were Ammonites and Moabites excluded from the assembly of the LORD, according to verse 4?

options.text: Because they did not meet Israel with food and water on the journey from Egypt, and hired Balaam to curse Israel.
options.note: Verse 4 states this explicit historical reason.

options.text: Because they worshiped on a different calendar.
options.note: The stated reason is their hostility during the exodus, not calendar differences.

options.text: Because they were too numerous.
options.note: The stated reason is historical hostility, not population size.

options.text: No reason is given for their exclusion.
options.note: Verse 4 gives an explicit historical reason.

quiz.q: What does the law say about a slave who has escaped and taken refuge with you?

options.text: Do not return him to his master; let him live among you wherever he chooses, without oppression.
options.note: Verses 15-16 state this explicitly.

options.text: You must return him immediately to avoid punishment.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids returning him.

options.text: You must sell him to someone else.
options.note: The text commands protection, not resale.

options.text: The law says nothing about this situation.
options.note: Verses 15-16 give explicit instruction.

quiz.q: What does the law say about charging interest on a loan to a fellow Israelite?

options.text: It is forbidden; you may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother.
options.note: Verses 19-20 state this explicit distinction.

options.text: Interest may be charged to anyone at any rate.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids interest to a fellow Israelite.

options.text: Interest is required on every loan.
options.note: The text forbids, rather than requires, interest among brothers.

options.text: The law does not address lending at all.
options.note: Verses 19-20 address it directly.

quiz.q: According to verses 21-23, what should a person do about a vow made to the LORD?

options.text: Keep it without delay, since God will require it, though it was never sinful to have refrained from vowing in the first place.
options.note: Verses 21-23 state this explicit principle.

options.text: Vows may be broken freely with no consequence.
options.note: Verse 21 explicitly warns that God will require it and count delay as sin.

options.text: Everyone is required to make vows regularly.
options.note: Verse 22 explicitly says refraining from a vow is not sinful.

options.text: The chapter has nothing to say about vows.
options.note: Verses 21-23 address vows directly.

quiz.q: What does the law permit when passing through a neighbor's vineyard or grainfield?

options.text: You may eat your fill by hand, but you must not harvest it with a basket or sickle to take away.
options.note: Verses 24-25 state this exact permission and limit.

options.text: You may harvest as much as you can carry to sell.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids using a basket or sickle to harvest for taking away.

options.text: You may not touch any of it under any circumstance.
options.note: The text explicitly permits eating your fill by hand.

options.text: The law is silent on this situation.
options.note: Verses 24-25 address it explicitly.

questions: This chapter protected a runaway slave rather than returning him to bondage. Who in your life has fled from a harmful situation, and how can you offer them the same kind of refuge rather than sending them back?
Israel was forbidden from charging a poor brother interest, since the loan was meant as covenant kindness, not profit. Where might your own generosity be quietly conditional on what you get back?
A vow to the LORD had to be kept exactly, even though making one was never required. Where have you made promises to God, or to others, that you have been slow to keep?
The eunuch was excluded here, yet Isaiah promised, and Acts fulfilled, his full welcome in God's house. Who do you find it hard to imagine God fully welcoming, and how does the gospel challenge that?
You were allowed to eat your fill from a neighbor's field but not to exploit it. Where is the line between enjoying what God provides through others' generosity and taking advantage of it?

translationNotes.note: The specific exclusions here concern eligibility for particular roles or full participation in Israel's covenant assembly under the old covenant; Isaiah 56:3-8 and Acts 8:26-39 show these very categories, the eunuch and the foreigner, explicitly welcomed under the gospel.

'Shrine prostitute' translates qedeshah, ironically built on the Hebrew word for 'holy'; Canaanite fertility religion twisted the language of holiness into cultic sex, which Israel's worship was to have nothing to do with.

The permission to charge foreigners interest but not brothers reflects the loan's purpose among Israelites as an act of covenant generosity to the poor, not commercial profit; it is not a general principle about how Israel was to treat foreigners in every matter.
